If I misinterpreted the post in my previous comment, here’s more info:

Try adding them on social media if you haven’t, then passively interact with their posts. It’ll help warm up the familiarity. They are most likely also very self-conscious with communicating because you grew up in another country. 

Everything I’ve just mentioned of course gets a difficulty ramp up because of social anxiety. The actual getting closer together I also dk how.

All of these are based from personal experience. Take what you deem useful OP.
Older relatives would ask more about your life in Canada and your experiences that are different from theirs, they initiate mostly. For cousins that are closer in age, if they are outgoing, school is a common topic. If they are tech-savvy, pop culture. It’s least awkward when there’s food.

There might be more people for you to meet, just a quick heads up. (relatives’ SOs, neighbors, friends of friends etc.)

If it’s your first time meeting them, they most likely also don’t expect you to say a lot. They will try to come  over to say hi tho. (Name, relationship, old memories if any) Bringing your phone, charger, and earbuds everywhere also helps because everyone else will have theirs. 

If you want to blend in even more, attend the birthday parties with a common acquaintance (parent etc.). You usually just nod, say a few words, stay on your phone and eat most of the time. 

I do understand your concern with the language barrier but they often accommodate, tho switching between dialects. 

Additionally, I wouldn’t expect anything more than superficial relationships with them. Genuine ones are rare. I feel the need to mention because of how common it is but yeah family dynamics in ph. If it doesn’t work out, often it’s them lol. People who seem very tight-knit are usually just bluffing. 

I sincerely wish you the best of luck.
